our_argument_summary: WIN-068 evaluates the dome's claim that the Kim & Chang (2018) 39-eclipse INTERMAGNET ensemble (1991-2016) confirms 'firmament-plate dielectric boundary shading.' Verdict: Std Model Explains. The Chapman (1919) ionospheric framework with modern conductivity treatment (Yamazaki & Maute 2017) plus the Kim & Chang ensemble produces the observed Y-increase / X-Z-F-decrease pattern at magnetic latitudes 30-50 over ~180-min windows without invoking dome geometry. FSF (delta_Z = baseline x coverage x H(r)/r) is properly routed to WIN-010 where it actually enters the predicted signal; the 39-eclipse ensemble counted here is a retrospective citation. Triple-counting critique (WIN-010 BOU 2017 + WIN-025 2024 9-station + WIN-068 1991-2016 ensemble = same Sq mechanism at three aggregation levels) and post-hoc critique (Kim & Chang 2018 published 8 years before V51.0 incorporation; monitor.py = 'none') are intact.

The dome relabels the same observed pattern as 'firmament-plate dielectric boundary shading' without an independent mechanism that predicts those specific features.

(FSF enters the separate 2026 forward projection at WIN-010, not here.)

holes_found.description: Finding overclaims 'predicts'. Current finding: 'the Chapman-Sq ionospheric framework ... together with the Kim & Chang (2018) ensemble predicts the 39-eclipse signal magnitude and geometry.' The detail_verdict_text and detail_evidence are careful to call Kim & Chang (2018) a 'retrospective citation' — strictly, the Chapman-Sq framework with measured conductivity inputs predicts the pattern; the Kim & Chang ensemble confirms the pattern across 39 events. Calling the ensemble itself 'predictive' is a minor wording tension that a defender could pull-quote ('your own review says Kim & Chang's retrospective analysis predicts the signal') to muddle the post-hoc point. The detail_verdict_text already nails this distinction; the finding should match.
holes_found.recommendation: Next finding touch: replace 'together with the Kim & Chang (2018) ensemble predicts the 39-eclipse signal magnitude and geometry' with 'predicts the eclipse magnetic pattern, and the Kim & Chang (2018) 39-eclipse ensemble confirms that pattern across 1991-2016 events.' Preserves the substance and aligns with detail_verdict_text framing. Low urgency; the detail panel carries the precise version.

holes_found.description: Triple-counting argument missing from finding. The cross-WIN consistency point — WIN-010/025/068 = same Sq mechanism at three aggregation levels (single-station, 9-station, 39-eclipse ensemble), counted as three separate WINs — is one of our strongest arguments and lives only in detail_evidence ¶4 and detail_verdict_text ¶5. A dome defender skimming the summary table sees three Std-Model-Explains rows and may infer they are three independent confirmations rather than three aggregation levels of one phenomenon. Finding is the row most readers see; it should carry at least a clause naming the triple-count.
holes_found.recommendation: Append to finding (after the FSF clause): ' Also one of three WINs (WIN-010 single-station, WIN-025 9-station, WIN-068 39-eclipse ensemble) counted separately for the same Sq mechanism at three aggregation levels.' stronger_arguments.description: Kim & Chang (2018) reports that the magnetic perturbation pattern was strongest at magnetic latitudes 30-50 — exactly the latitude band where the standard model's Sq vortex is most intense (Yamazaki & Maute 2017). The dome's cavity mechanism has no a priori reason to peak at those particular magnetic latitudes; it would generically predict peak at geometric distance from disc center. The latitude-dependence specifically is a structural Sq feature, not a generic 'magnetic effect during eclipse' feature. Could be added to detail_evidence as a sharper discriminator.
sources: Yamazaki & Maute 2017 Sq vortex latitude dependence

kernel_of_truth.description: Kim & Chang (2018, Adv. Space Res. 61:2040-2049, S0273117718300656) is a rigorous, peer-reviewed statistical study of real geomagnetic observations during 39 eclipses across 25 years — there is no question that eclipse magnetic perturbations are real, systematic, and reproducible. The dome correctly identifies a real published dataset (data/wins.json:detail_evidence ¶1) and correctly notes that the perturbation magnitude and pattern are statistically significant across the ensemble. The phenomenon being cited is genuine.
kernel_of_truth.why_it_doesnt_save_claim: What the dome cannot do is derive the specific component pattern (Y-up / X-Z-F-down), the latitude band (30-50 magnetic), the 180-min window, OR the magnitude from its cavity geometry. The standard model derives all four from the Sq dynamo + measured ionospheric conductivity (data/wins.json:detail_evidence ¶3, citing Yamazaki & Maute 2017). The dome reuses the observed pattern as a 'prediction' without an independent derivation chain. Worse, the FSF scaling law that the dome does derive (data/wins.json:detail_verdict_text ¶2) is not invoked anywhere in the 39-eclipse ensemble evaluated here — it only enters the 2026 forward projection at WIN-010. A confirmed phenomenon does not become a dome prediction just by being cited.

The verdict (Std Model Explains) has held since 2026-04-13 across c12-c16, which is what we want — the verdict_history note in detail_extra still documents the brief 2026-04-12/-04-13 flip-pair for audit transparency. advocate_mode.best_defense: A capable dome defender would argue: 'You concede Kim & Chang (2018) is a rigorous study of real perturbations. You concede the dome correctly publishes a scaling equation (FSF = H(r)/r) and you yourselves verified Pearson r = 0.9999 in WIN-010 — meaning the dome derives genuine geometric structure between stations. The fact that the 1991-2016 ensemble is a retrospective citation does not erase the fact that the dome has a quantitative, dome-derived geometric scaling law that holds across observatories. Your verdict text routes the FSF discussion to WIN-010 to avoid double-relitigating, but the Steelman intent here is that WIN-068 should count as a confirmed observation of the phenomenon class that the dome geometrically scales. Your Std Model Explains verdict treats the dome's contribution as zero, when the dome genuinely contributes the inter-station ratio law — even if it does not contribute the absolute magnitude or the underlying photoionization mechanism. A fairer verdict tag would be Partial Credit or Non-Discriminating, not Std Model Explains.'

quantitative_verification.computations: Ran node compute: H(0)=8537.0, H(20015)=837.1, linear-radial average 3315.8 km, quarter-wave f=22.60 Hz. These reproduce the WIN-002 detail_evidence numerical claims (linear avg 3316 km, ~22.6 Hz) to better than rounding precision.
